output.method: Use a roots-of-unity filter on the weighted counting polynomials. The decisive hypothesis is that the three-step transfer matrix at a primitive cube root has trace 1 and determinant −1; direct symbolic multiplication establishes this, rather than fitting a recurrence to data. Its characteristic identity gives an exact recurrence for the nontrivial Fourier terms and shows that their growth is strictly slower than Fibonacci growth. All calculations below are algebraic; no runtime or external verification was available. Minimality of the recurrence and literature novelty are not claimed.

reasoning_steps.title: Weighted counting and the roots-of-unity filter
reasoning_steps.argument: For n≥0, let P_n(q)=Σ_S q^{Σ_{i∈S}i}, where S ranges over subsets of {1,…,n} containing no consecutive elements. The empty subset contributes 1. Separating sets according to whether they contain n gives P_n(q)=P_{n−1}(q)+q^nP_{n−2}(q) for n≥2, with P_0(q)=1 and P_1(q)=1+q. Set P_{−1}(q)=1 as an auxiliary convention, so the same identity also holds for n=1. Let ω be a primitive cube root of unity. For every integer s, (1+ω^s+ω^{2s})/3 equals 1 if 3 divides s and 0 otherwise. Applying this identity to each subset gives 3a_n=P_n(1)+P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²). At q=1, the recurrence and initial values give P_n(1)=F_{n+2}.

reasoning_steps.title: Exact three-step transfer identity
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix q∈{ω,ω²}, write p_n=P_n(q), and set v_n=(p_n,p_{n−1})ᵀ for n≥0. Then v_j=M_jv_{j−1}, where M_j=[[1,q^j],[1,0]] for j≥1. Put T_n=M_{n+3}M_{n+2}M_{n+1}. Writing α=q^{n+1}, β=q^{n+2}, γ=q^{n+3}, direct multiplication yields T_n=[[1+β+γ,α(1+γ)],[1+β,α]]. The three powers α,β,γ are 1,q,q² in some order, so tr(T_n)=1+α+β+γ=1 and det(T_n)=−αβγ=−1. Thus the characteristic identity is T_n²−T_n−I=0.

reasoning_steps.title: A universal recurrence for the nontrivial Fourier terms
reasoning_steps.argument: Because M_{j+3}=M_j, we have T_{n+3}=T_n. Consequently v_{n+6}=T_n²v_n=T_nv_n+v_n=v_{n+3}+v_n for every n≥0. Taking first components proves P_{n+6}(q)=P_{n+3}(q)+P_n(q), including n=0 because of the auxiliary P_{−1}=1 convention. Therefore b_n:=P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²)=3a_n−F_{n+2} satisfies b_{n+6}=b_{n+3}+b_n for all n≥0.

reasoning_steps.title: Deriving the integer-coefficient recurrence
reasoning_steps.argument: Let E denote the forward shift. The sequence f_n=F_{n+2} is annihilated by L(E)=E²−E−1, and b_n is annihilated by H(E)=E⁶−E³−1. Since polynomial shift operators commute, L(E)H(E) annihilates f+b=3a and hence a. Expanding gives L(x)H(x)=x⁸−x⁷−x⁶−x⁵+x⁴+x³−x²+x+1. Thus, for every n≥0, a_{n+8}−a_{n+7}−a_{n+6}−a_{n+5}+a_{n+4}+a_{n+3}−a_{n+2}+a_{n+1}+a_n=0. This proves the claimed recurrence without any pattern-fitting assumption.

reasoning_steps.title: Sufficient initial values
reasoning_steps.argument: Using 1+ω+ω²=0 in the weighted recurrence gives (P_0(ω),…,P_5(ω))=(1,1+ω,0,1+ω,1+ω,1). Adding the conjugate values gives (b_0,…,b_5)=(2,1,0,1,1,2). The proved six-step recurrence then gives b_6=3 and b_7=2. Since (F_2,…,F_9)=(1,2,3,5,8,13,21,34), the identity a_n=(F_{n+2}+b_n)/3 gives (a_0,…,a_7)=(1,1,1,2,3,5,8,12). These eight values uniquely determine the sequence under the order-eight recurrence.

reasoning_steps.title: Exact evaluation at n=12
reasoning_steps.argument: The b recurrence gives b_6=b_3+b_0=3, b_9=b_6+b_3=4, and b_12=b_9+b_6=7. Fibonacci iteration gives F_14=377. Therefore a_12=(377+7)/3=128. As a separate finite arithmetic check, let C_n=(c_{n,0},c_{n,1},c_{n,2}) count admissible subsets by sum residue. The include/exclude bijection gives c_{n,r}=c_{n−1,r}+c_{n−2,r−n mod 3}, with C_0=(1,0,0), C_1=(1,1,0). Iteration gives C_2=(1,1,1), C_3=(2,2,1), C_4=(3,3,2), C_5=(5,4,4), C_6=(8,7,6), C_7=(12,12,10), C_8=(19,18,18), C_9=(31,30,28), C_10=(49,49,46), C_11=(79,77,77), and C_12=(128,126,123). Its first coordinate agrees, and its coordinates sum to 377.

reasoning_steps.title: Strictly smaller growth and the limiting proportion
reasoning_steps.argument: For each r∈{0,1,2}, the sequence k↦b_{3k+r} satisfies the Fibonacci recurrence. Its initial pairs are (2,1), (1,1), and (0,2), respectively. Checking those pairs and then using recurrence uniqueness proves, for every k≥0, b_{3k}=2F_{k+1}−F_k, b_{3k+1}=F_{k+1}, and b_{3k+2}=2F_k. Let φ=(1+√5)/2 and ψ=(1−√5)/2. The expression (φ^m−ψ^m)/√5 satisfies the Fibonacci recurrence and its two initial values, so it equals F_m. Since |ψ|<1, the displayed formulas imply b_n=O(φ^{n/3}), whereas F_{n+2} is asymptotic to φ^{n+2}/√5. Hence b_n/F_{n+2}=O(φ^{−2n/3})→0. Finally a_n/F_{n+2}=1/3+b_n/(3F_{n+2})→1/3.

output.method: Derive the proposed gap-removal Gaussian-binomial formula, then evaluate it at primitive cube roots using a coefficient identity proved directly from a finite product. This tests the hypothesis that the root-of-unity contributions reduce to Fibonacci numbers on each residue class. A discrepancy in any of the three residue classes would refute that reduction; instead, the resulting formulas also satisfy the independently derived weighted-Fibonacci recurrence in every phase. All calculations below are exact symbolic deductions, not fitted computational patterns. Neither execution runtime is available, and no external sources are needed or claimed inspected.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the weighted count and prove the gap-removal formula
reasoning_steps.argument: Let P_n(q)=∑_S q^{∑_{i∈S}i}, summing over subsets S⊆{1,…,n} with no consecutive elements; P_0(q)=1. For N≥0 and 0≤k≤N, define the Gaussian polynomial G_{N,k}(q)=∑_{0≤j_1<⋯<j_k<N}q^{∑j_h−k(k−1)/2}. Its defining sum gives ∏_{j=0}^{N−1}(1+zq^j)=∑_{k=0}^N z^k q^{k(k−1)/2}G_{N,k}(q). For a nonconsecutive k-subset i_1<⋯<i_k, put y_j=i_j−(j−1). This is a bijection with k-subsets of {1,…,n−k+1}: the inverse i_j=y_j+j−1 has gaps at least two. Setting j_h=y_h−1 shows ∑i_h=∑j_h+k(k+1)/2, so its enumerator is q^{k²}G_{n−k+1,k}(q). Thus P_n(q)=∑_{k=0}^{⌊(n+1)/2⌋}q^{k²}G_{n−k+1,k}(q), including the empty term k=0.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the cube-root Gaussian-binomial reduction
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix ω with ω³=1 and ω≠1, so 1+ω+ω²=0. For N=3M+s, 0≤s≤2, the product above becomes ∏_{j=0}^{N−1}(1+zω^j)=(1+z³)^M∏_{j=0}^{s−1}(1+zω^j), because (1+z)(1+zω)(1+zω²)=1+z³. Compare coefficients of z^{3ℓ+t}, 0≤t≤2. The residual product has degree at most two, so its only possible contributing degree is t. Also (3ℓ+t)(3ℓ+t−1)/2−t(t−1)/2 is divisible by three. Consequently G_{3M+s,3ℓ+t}(ω)=binom(M,ℓ)G_{s,t}(ω), where G_{s,t}=0 for t>s. This proves the needed root-of-unity identity rather than assuming a q-Lucas theorem.

reasoning_steps.title: Evaluate all three residue classes
reasoning_steps.argument: Use binom(A,ℓ)=0 unless A≥ℓ≥0, and set S_m=∑_{ℓ≥0}binom(m−ℓ,ℓ) for m≥0, with S_{−1}=0. Pascal's identity gives S_m=S_{m−1}+S_{m−2} for m≥2; S_0=S_1=1, hence S_m=F_{m+1}. In the gap-removal sum, write n=3m+r and k=3ℓ+t. Then ω^{k²} is 1 for t=0 and ω for t=1,2. Applying the preceding coefficient identity gives the following contributions from t=0,1,2 respectively: for r=0, S_m, 0, ωS_{m−1}; for r=1, S_m, ωS_m, 0; for r=2, S_{m+1}, −S_m, 0. For example, the r=2,t=1 term uses G_{2,1}(ω)=1+ω and ω(1+ω)=−1. The zero-binomial convention handles all excluded k, and S_{−1}=0 handles n=0. Therefore P_{3m}(ω)=F_{m+1}+ωF_m, P_{3m+1}(ω)=(1+ω)F_{m+1}, and P_{3m+2}(ω)=F_m for every m≥0.

reasoning_steps.title: Check the formulas by a separate combinatorial recurrence
reasoning_steps.argument: Partitioning admissible subsets according to whether n is selected gives P_n(q)=P_{n−1}(q)+q^nP_{n−2}(q) for n≥2, with P_0(q)=1 and P_1(q)=1+q. In particular P_2=1+q+q² and P_3=1+q+q²+q³+q⁴, agreeing with direct enumeration and gap removal. Write p_n=P_n(ω). The closed formulas satisfy all three phases of this recurrence: for m≥1, p_{3m}+ωp_{3m−1}=F_{m+1}+ω(F_m+F_{m−1})=(1+ω)F_{m+1}; for m≥0, p_{3m+1}+ω²p_{3m}=(1+ω+ω²)F_{m+1}+F_m=F_m; and p_{3m+2}+p_{3m+1}=F_{m+2}+ωF_{m+1}. Together with p_0=1 and p_1=1+ω, this independently checks every index, not just multiples of three.

reasoning_steps.title: Extract the counts divisible by three
reasoning_steps.argument: For every integer h, (1+ω^h+ω^{2h})/3 equals 1 if 3 divides h and 0 otherwise. Thus 3a_n=P_n(1)+P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²). The unweighted recurrence gives P_n(1)=F_{n+2}, including n=0,1. Since P_n has real integer coefficients, P_n(ω²) is the conjugate of P_n(ω). Taking the sum of the explicit formulas and their conjugates yields c_{3m}=2F_{m+1}−F_m, c_{3m+1}=F_{m+1}, and c_{3m+2}=2F_m, where c_n=P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²). Hence 3a_n=F_{n+2}+c_n exactly.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the integer constant-coefficient recurrence
reasoning_steps.argument: Each of the three residue-class formulas for c_n is a fixed linear combination of F_m and F_{m+1}. Therefore c_{n+6}=c_{n+3}+c_n for every n≥0. Let E denote the forward shift, (Eu)_n=u_{n+1}. The Fibonacci component is annihilated by E²−E−1 and c is annihilated by E⁶−E³−1. Since shift polynomials commute, their product annihilates 3a and hence a. Expanding gives (E²−E−1)(E⁶−E³−1)=E⁸−E⁷−E⁶−E⁵+E⁴+E³−E²+E+1. Rearrangement proves a_{n+8}=a_{n+7}+a_{n+6}+a_{n+5}−a_{n+4}−a_{n+3}+a_{n+2}−a_{n+1}−a_n for all n≥0. No minimal-order claim is needed.

reasoning_steps.title: Supply sufficient initial values and compute a_12
reasoning_steps.argument: For n=0,…,7 the Fibonacci component F_{n+2} is (1,2,3,5,8,13,21,34), while the correction c_n is (2,1,0,1,1,2,3,2). Their sums divided by three give (a_0,…,a_7)=(1,1,1,2,3,5,8,12), sufficient for the order-eight recurrence. At n=12=3·4, c_12=2F_5−F_4=2·5−3=7 and F_14=377. Therefore a_12=(377+7)/3=128.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the limiting density
reasoning_steps.argument: Let φ=(1+√5)/2, so φ²=φ+1. Induction on the Fibonacci recurrence gives F_j≤φ^j for j≥0 and F_{n+2}≥φ^n for n≥0; the latter starts from F_2=1 and F_3=2≥φ. Put m=⌊n/3⌋. The three correction formulas imply |c_n|≤3φ^{m+1}. Consequently |a_n/F_{n+2}−1/3|=|c_n|/(3F_{n+2})≤φ^{m+1−n}. Since m+1−n≤1−2n/3 tends to minus infinity, the bound tends to zero. This establishes the limit without assuming equidistribution.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the weighted enumerator and justify gap removal
reasoning_steps.argument: For n≥0, let P_n(q)=∑_S q^{∑_{i∈S}i}, where S ranges over subsets of {1,…,n} having no consecutive elements. The empty subset contributes 1. Define G_{N,k}(q)=∑_{0≤j_1<⋯<j_k<N}q^{∑j_h−k(k−1)/2}, the Gaussian binomial polynomial, with G_{N,0}=1. For a nonconsecutive k-subset i_1<⋯<i_k, the transformation y_h=i_h−(h−1) is a bijection onto ordinary k-subsets of {1,…,n−k+1}: its inverse i_h=y_h+h−1 has gaps at least two. Writing j_h=y_h−1 gives ∑i_h=∑j_h+k(k+1)/2. Combining this shift with the Gaussian normalization gives P_n(q)=∑_{k=0}^{⌊(n+1)/2⌋}q^{k²}G_{n−k+1,k}(q). This includes n=0 and k=0.

reasoning_steps.title: Obtain an exact recurrence and the total number of admissible subsets
reasoning_steps.argument: Partition the subsets according to whether n is selected. Excluding n leaves an arbitrary admissible subset on n−1 positions. Including n forces n−1 to be absent; removing n leaves an arbitrary admissible subset on n−2 positions and removes weight q^n. These disjoint reversible constructions prove P_n(q)=P_{n−1}(q)+q^nP_{n−2}(q) for n≥2, with P_0(q)=1 and P_1(q)=1+q. At q=1 this is the Fibonacci recurrence with initial values 1,2, so P_n(1)=F_{n+2}. For low-index checks, P_2(q)=1+q+q² and P_3(q)=1+q+q²+q³+q⁴, agreeing with direct enumeration.

reasoning_steps.title: Evaluate the cube-root contribution in every phase
reasoning_steps.argument: Let ω be a primitive cube root of unity, so 1+ω+ω²=0, and put p_n=P_n(ω). We prove, for all m≥0, p_{3m}=F_{m+1}+ωF_m, p_{3m+1}=(1+ω)F_{m+1}, and p_{3m+2}=F_m. The base triple is p_0=1, p_1=1+ω, p_2=0, matching F_0=0 and F_1=F_2=1. Suppose the formulas hold for m. The weighted recurrence gives p_{3m+3}=p_{3m+2}+p_{3m+1}=F_{m+2}+ωF_{m+1}. Next, p_{3m+4}=p_{3m+3}+ωp_{3m+2}=F_{m+2}+ω(F_{m+1}+F_m)=(1+ω)F_{m+2}. Finally, p_{3m+5}=p_{3m+4}+ω²p_{3m+3}=(1+ω+ω²)F_{m+2}+ω³F_{m+1}=F_{m+1}. Thus the complete next triple follows, proving all phases and all nonnegative indices.

reasoning_steps.title: Extract exactly the subsets whose sums are divisible by three
reasoning_steps.argument: For every integer h, (1+ω^h+ω^{2h})/3 is 1 when 3 divides h and 0 otherwise. Applying this identity termwise to the finite polynomial gives 3a_n=P_n(1)+P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²). Since P_n has integer coefficients, P_n(ω²) is the complex conjugate of P_n(ω). Define c_n=P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²). The formulas just proved and ω+ω²=−1 yield c_{3m}=2F_{m+1}−F_m, c_{3m+1}=F_{m+1}, and c_{3m+2}=2F_m. Consequently 3a_n=F_{n+2}+c_n exactly, including n=0 and the empty subset.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the constant-coefficient integer recurrence
reasoning_steps.argument: For each fixed residue r∈{0,1,2}, c_{3m+r} is a fixed linear combination of F_m and F_{m+1}. Hence c_{n+6}=c_{n+3}+c_n for every n≥0. Let E denote the forward shift, (Eu)_n=u_{n+1}. The sequences F_{n+2} and c_n are annihilated respectively by E²−E−1 and E⁶−E³−1. These shift polynomials commute, so their product annihilates their sum 3a_n and therefore a_n. Expanding gives (E²−E−1)(E⁶−E³−1)=E⁸−E⁷−E⁶−E⁵+E⁴+E³−E²+E+1. Thus, for every n≥0, a_{n+8}=a_{n+7}+a_{n+6}+a_{n+5}−a_{n+4}−a_{n+3}+a_{n+2}−a_{n+1}−a_n. Minimal order is not needed or claimed.

reasoning_steps.title: Give sufficient initial values and compute a_12
reasoning_steps.argument: For n=0,…,7, the values of F_{n+2} are (1,2,3,5,8,13,21,34), and the correction formulas give c_n=(2,1,0,1,1,2,3,2). Taking their sums and dividing by three gives (a_0,…,a_7)=(1,1,1,2,3,5,8,12). These eight consecutive values suffice because the recurrence is monic of order eight. At n=12=3·4, c_12=2F_5−F_4=10−3=7 and F_14=377, so a_12=(377+7)/3=128. As an arithmetic consistency check, the proved scalar recurrence gives a_8,…,a_12=(19,31,49,79,128).

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the limiting density with an exponential error bound
reasoning_steps.argument: Let φ=(1+√5)/2, so φ²=φ+1. For each r∈{0,1,2}, set b_m=c_{3m+r}. Its recurrence is b_{m+2}=b_{m+1}+b_m. The initial pairs are (2,1), (1,1), and (0,2), respectively, so |b_0|≤2 and |b_1|≤2φ. Induction using the triangle inequality gives |b_m|≤2φ^m: the induction step is 2φ^{m+1}+2φ^m=2φ^{m+2}. Separating sets according to whether they contain n gives P_n(q)=P_{n−1}(q)+q^nP_{n−2}(q) for n≥2, with P_0(q)=1 and P_1(q)=1+q. Set P_{−1}(q)=1 as an auxiliary convention, so the same identity also holds for n=1. Let ω be a primitive cube root of unity. For every integer s, (1+ω^s+ω^{2s})/3 equals 1 if 3 divides s and 0 otherwise. Applying this identity to each subset gives 3a_n=P_n(1)+P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²). At q=1, the recurrence and initial values give P_n(1)=F_{n+2}.

reasoning_steps.argument: Fix q∈{ω,ω²}, write p_n=P_n(q), and set v_n=(p_n,p_{n−1})ᵀ for n≥0. Then v_j=M_jv_{j−1}, where M_j=[[1,q^j],[1,0]] for j≥1. Put T_n=M_{n+3}M_{n+2}M_{n+1}. argument_steps.title: Weighted counting and the roots-of-unity filter
argument_steps.argument: For n≥0, let P_n(q)=Σ_S q^{Σ_{i∈S}i}, where S ranges over subsets of {1,…,n} containing no consecutive elements. The empty subset contributes 1. Separating sets according to whether they contain n gives P_n(q)=P_{n−1}(q)+q^nP_{n−2}(q) for n≥2, with P_0(q)=1 and P_1(q)=1+q. Set P_{−1}(q)=1 as an auxiliary convention, so the same identity also holds for n=1. Let ω be a primitive cube root of unity. For every integer s, (1+ω^s+ω^{2s})/3 equals 1 if 3 divides s and 0 otherwise. Applying this identity to each subset gives 3a_n=P_n(1)+P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²). At q=1, the recurrence and initial values give P_n(1)=F_{n+2}.

review.rationale: Removing n from a subset that contains it leaves an arbitrary admissible subset of {1,…,n−2}, with weight multiplied by q^n. The auxiliary P_{−1}=1 makes the n=1 identity valid. argument_steps.title: Exact three-step transfer identity

Writing α=q^{n+1}, β=q^{n+2}, γ=q^{n+3}, direct multiplication yields T_n=[[1+β+γ,α(1+γ)],[1+β,α]]. The three powers α,β,γ are 1,q,q² in some order, so tr(T_n)=1+α+β+γ=1 and det(T_n)=−αβγ=−1. Thus the characteristic identity is T_n²−T_n−I=0.

Therefore b_n:=P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²)=3a_n−F_{n+2} satisfies b_{n+6}=b_{n+3}+b_n for all n≥0.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the weighted count and prove the gap-removal formula
reasoning_steps.argument: Let P_n(q)=∑_S q^{∑_{i∈S}i}, summing over subsets S⊆{1,…,n} with no consecutive elements; P_0(q)=1. For N≥0 and 0≤k≤N, define the Gaussian polynomial G_{N,k}(q)=∑_{0≤j_1<⋯<j_k<N}q^{∑j_h−k(k−1)/2}. Its defining sum gives ∏_{j=0}^{N−1}(1+zq^j)=∑_{k=0}^N z^k q^{k(k−1)/2}G_{N,k}(q). For a nonconsecutive k-subset i_1<⋯<i_k, put y_j=i_j−(j−1). This is a bijection with k-subsets of {1,…,n−k+1}: the inverse i_j=y_j+j−1 has gaps at least two. Setting j_h=y_h−1 shows ∑i_h=∑j_h+k(k+1)/2, so its enumerator is q^{k²}G_{n−k+1,k}(q). Thus P_n(q)=∑_{k=0}^{⌊(n+1)/2⌋}q^{k²}G_{n−k+1,k}(q), including the empty term k=0.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the cube-root Gaussian-binomial reduction
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix ω with ω³=1 and ω≠1, so 1+ω+ω²=0. For N=3M+s, 0≤s≤2, the product above becomes ∏_{j=0}^{N−1}(1+zω^j)=(1+z³)^M∏_{j=0}^{s−1}(1+zω^j), because (1+z)(1+zω)(1+zω²)=1+z³. Compare coefficients of z^{3ℓ+t}, 0≤t≤2. The residual product has degree at most two, so its only possible contributing degree is t. Also (3ℓ+t)(3ℓ+t−1)/2−t(t−1)/2 is divisible by three. Consequently G_{3M+s,3ℓ+t}(ω)=binom(M,ℓ)G_{s,t}(ω), where G_{s,t}=0 for t>s. This proves the needed root-of-unity identity rather than assuming a q-Lucas theorem.

reasoning_steps.argument: Use binom(A,ℓ)=0 unless A≥ℓ≥0, and set S_m=∑_{ℓ≥0}binom(m−ℓ,ℓ) for m≥0, with S_{−1}=0. Pascal's identity gives S_m=S_{m−1}+S_{m−2} for m≥2; S_0=S_1=1, hence S_m=F_{m+1}. In the gap-removal sum, write n=3m+r and k=3ℓ+t. Then ω^{k²} is 1 for t=0 and ω for t=1,2. Applying the preceding coefficient identity gives the following contributions from t=0,1,2 respectively: for r=0, S_m, 0, ωS_{m−1}; for r=1, S_m, ωS_m, 0; for r=2, S_{m+1}, −S_m, 0. For example, the r=2,t=1 term uses G_{2,1}(ω)=1+ω and ω(1+ω)=−1. The zero-binomial convention handles all excluded k, and S_{−1}=0 handles n=0. Therefore P_{3m}(ω)=F_{m+1}+ωF_m, P_{3m+1}(ω)=(1+ω)F_{m+1}, and P_{3m+2}(ω)=F_m for every m≥0.

In particular P_2=1+q+q² and P_3=1+q+q²+q³+q⁴, agreeing with direct enumeration and gap removal. Write p_n=P_n(ω). The closed formulas satisfy all three phases of this recurrence: for m≥1, p_{3m}+ωp_{3m−1}=F_{m+1}+ω(F_m+F_{m−1})=(1+ω)F_{m+1}; for m≥0, p_{3m+1}+ω²p_{3m}=(1+ω+ω²)F_{m+1}+F_m=F_m; and p_{3m+2}+p_{3m+1}=F_{m+2}+ωF_{m+1}. Together with p_0=1 and p_1=1+ω, this independently checks every index, not just multiples of three.

Each d_n has coordinate sum zero. Because T1=1, subtraction of the total-count recurrence gives d_n=d_{n−1}+T^n d_{n−2}. Its first coordinate c_n satisfies c_n=3a_n−F_{n+2}. Thus it remains to control a zero-sum integer vector, not to assume equidistribution.

review.rationale: Coordinate summation removes the residue permutation and gives the Fibonacci recurrence with initial totals 1 and 2. Since T fixes the all-ones vector, subtracting that total recurrence gives the asserted recurrence for d_n, whose coordinate sum is zero. Its first coordinate is exactly 3a_n−F_{n+2}.

argument_steps.title: Derive the three-step transition exactly
argument_steps.argument: For a linear operator A define M(A)=[[I,A],[I,0]], acting on pairs of three-vectors. Then (d_n,d_{n−1})^T=M(T^n)(d_{n−1},d_{n−2})^T. Since T^3=I, the state w_m=(d_{3m+1},d_{3m})^T obeys w_{m+1}=Bw_m for m≥0, where B=M(T)M(I)M(T²)=[[2I+T,I+T²],[2I,T²]]. This multiplication uses the transitions at indices 3m+2, 3m+3 and 3m+4 in their chronological order.

review.rationale: The transitions from index 3m+1 to 3m+4 apply M(T²), M(I), and M(T), in that order. Direct block multiplication gives B=[[2I+T,I+T²],[2I,T²]], including the initial transition m=0.

argument_steps.title: Prove the decisive transition identity on the correct subspace
argument_steps.argument: Let W be the subspace of three-vectors with coordinate sum zero. For x∈W, (I+T+T²)x=0, since each coordinate of that sum equals the coordinate sum of x. Hence on W, T²=−I−T and B=[[2I+T,−T],[2I,−I−T]]. Its blocks commute. For any commuting blocks A,C,D,E, direct multiplication gives [[A,C],[D,E]]²−(A+E)[[A,C],[D,E]]+(AE−CD)I_pair=0. Here A+E=I and AE−CD=(2I+T)(−I−T)+2T=−I, using T²=−I−T. Consequently B²−B−I_pair=0 on W×W. The zero-sum restriction is essential: on the constant-vector subspace, the corresponding block trace is 4I rather than I.

review.rationale: On the zero-sum subspace, I+T+T² vanishes. All blocks are polynomials in T and therefore commute. Substituting T²=−I−T gives block trace I and determinant (2I+T)(−I−T)+2T=−I; the displayed block identity consequently yields B²−B−I=0. The explicit restriction avoids incorrectly applying this identity to the constant-vector component.

argument_steps.title: Obtain the imbalance recurrence in all three phases
argument_steps.argument: Since w_m∈W×W, the identity just proved implies w_{m+2}=w_{m+1}+w_m. Its two coordinates give d_{3m+7}=d_{3m+4}+d_{3m+1} and d_{3m+6}=d_{3m+3}+d_{3m}. For the missing phase, d_{3m+2}=d_{3m+1}+T²d_{3m}; applying this fixed linear map to the recurrence for w_m yields d_{3m+8}=d_{3m+5}+d_{3m+2}. Thus d_{n+6}=d_{n+3}+d_n, and therefore c_{n+6}=c_{n+3}+c_n, for every n≥0. This establishes the proposed identity globally, including n=0,1,2.

review.rationale: Applying the quadratic identity to w_m establishes the recurrence for residue-index phases 0 and 1. The fixed map (u,v)↦u+T²v gives phase 2, so no phase is omitted. Every resulting index is nonnegative, and the argument includes n=0,1,2.

argument_steps.title: Derive an integer constant-coefficient recurrence for a_n
argument_steps.argument: Let E be the forward shift on sequences. The sequence t_n=F_{n+2} is annihilated by E²−E−1, and c_n is annihilated by E⁶−E³−1. Since these shift polynomials commute, their product annihilates 3a_n=t_n+c_n. Expanding gives (E²−E−1)(E⁶−E³−1)=E⁸−E⁷−E⁶−E⁵+E⁴+E³−E²+E+1. Expanding the product gives E⁸−E⁷−E⁶−E⁵+E⁴+E³−E²+E+1, with exactly the stated recurrence signs. Division by 3 is legitimate over these integer-valued sequences.

reasoning_steps.title: Counting polynomials and an exact filter
reasoning_steps.argument: Define P_n(q)=Σ_S q^{Σ_{i∈S}i}, summing over admissible subsets. Excluding n contributes P_{n−1}(q); including n forbids n−1 and contributes q^nP_{n−2}(q). Hence P_n=P_{n−1}+q^nP_{n−2} for n≥2, with P_0=1 and P_1=1+q. For a primitive cube root q, the identity 1+q^s+q^{2s}=3 when 3 divides s and zero otherwise proves 3a_n=P_n(1)+P_n(q)+P_n(q²). At q=1 the recurrence and initial values give P_n(1)=F_{n+2}. This is a sum-residue filter, not coefficient extraction at a root.

reasoning_steps.title: Formal functional equations replace transfer matrices
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix q with q³=1 and q≠1, and write G(x)=Σ_{n≥0}P_n(q)x^n in Q(q)[[x]]. Summing the counting recurrence for n≥2 gives (1−x)G(x)=1+qx+q²x²G(qx). Replacing x successively by qx and q²x gives (1−qx)G(qx)=1+q²x+qx²G(q²x) and (1−q²x)G(q²x)=1+x+x²G(x). These equations include both initial terms explicitly and require no negative-index convention.

reasoning_steps.title: Exact elimination of the three equations
reasoning_steps.argument: Substituting the last two functional equations into the first and multiplying through by (1−qx)(1−q²x) yields [(1−x)(1−qx)(1−q²x)−x⁶]G(x)=(1+qx)(1−qx)(1−q²x)+q²x²(1+q²x)(1−q²x)+x⁴(1+x). Since q³=1 and 1+q+q²=0, the left multiplier is 1−x³−x⁶. Expanding the right side gives 1−q²x+qx³+x⁵. Therefore G(x)=(1−q²x+qx³+x⁵)/(1−x³−x⁶). Every denominator used has constant term one and is thus invertible as a formal series; no analytic convergence assumption enters.

reasoning_steps.title: The scalar generating function
reasoning_steps.argument: Let b_n=P_n(q)+P_n(q²) and B(x)=Σ b_nx^n. Adding the conjugate rational identities gives B(x)=(2+x−x³+2x⁵)/(1−x³−x⁶). Also Σ F_{n+2}x^n=(1+x)/(1−x−x²), as follows by multiplying by 1−x−x² and checking the first two coefficients. The filter now gives 3A(x)=(1+x)/(1−x−x²)+(2+x−x³+2x⁵)/(1−x³−x⁶). Combining fractions and expanding the numerator proves A(x)=N(x)/D(x), where N=1−x²−x³+x⁵−x⁶−x⁷ and D=1−x−x²−x³+x⁴+x⁵−x⁶+x⁷+x⁸.

reasoning_steps.title: Universal recurrence and sufficient initial values
reasoning_steps.argument: Since D(x)A(x)=N(x) and deg N=7, every coefficient of degree n+8, n≥0, is zero. Thus a_{n+8}−a_{n+7}−a_{n+6}−a_{n+5}+a_{n+4}+a_{n+3}−a_{n+2}+a_{n+1}+a_n=0. For an integer-only initial check, let C_n=(c_{n,0},c_{n,1},c_{n,2}) count subsets by their sum residue. The same include/exclude bijection proves c_{n,r}=c_{n−1,r}+c_{n−2,(r−n) mod 3} for n≥2, with C_0=(1,0,0), C_1=(1,1,0). It gives C_2=(1,1,1), C_3=(2,2,1), C_4=(3,3,2), C_5=(5,4,4), C_6=(8,7,6), C_7=(12,12,10). The first coordinates supply (a_0,…,a_7)=(1,1,1,2,3,5,8,12), which uniquely determine the sequence under the monic order-eight recurrence. These are exact finite calculations from a proved counting identity, not a fitted recurrence.

reasoning_steps.argument: The identity (1−x³−x⁶)B(x)=2+x−x³+2x⁵ gives (b_0,…,b_5)=(2,1,0,1,1,2) and b_{n+6}=b_{n+3}+b_n for all n≥0. Consequently b_6=3, b_9=4, b_12=7. Separately continuing the residue-count recurrence gives C_8=(19,18,18), C_9=(31,30,28), C_10=(49,49,46), C_11=(79,77,77), and C_12=(128,126,123). Its first coordinate is 128 and its coordinate sum is 377. This is a different arithmetic route, although both routes originate in the same include/exclude bijection.

reasoning_steps.title: Strictly smaller correction and the limit
reasoning_steps.argument: For each r∈{0,1,2}, the sequence k↦b_{3k+r} satisfies the Fibonacci recurrence. Its initial pairs, obtained above, are respectively (2,1), (1,1), and (0,2). Checking these pairs and applying induction therefore gives b_{3k}=2F_{k+1}−F_k, b_{3k+1}=F_{k+1}, and b_{3k+2}=2F_k for all k≥0, including k=0. Put φ=(1+√5)/2 and ψ=(1−√5)/2. Both roots satisfy t²=t+1; thus (φ^m−ψ^m)/√5 satisfies the Fibonacci recurrence and initial values and equals F_m. Because |ψ|<1<φ, the displayed formulas give b_n=O(φ^{n/3}), while F_{n+2} is asymptotic to φ^{n+2}/√5. Therefore a_n/F_{n+2}=1/3+b_n/(3F_{n+2})=1/3+O(φ^{−2n/3})→1/3. The denominator F_{n+2} is positive for every n≥0.

reasoning_steps.title: A new check: the denominator cannot cancel
reasoning_steps.argument: Write L=1−x−x², H=1−x³−x⁶, and T=2+x−x³+2x⁵, so 3N=(1+x)H+TL. Reduction modulo two gives L̄=1+x+x², H̄=1+x³+x⁶, and T̄=x+x³=x(x+1)². Modulo L̄ we have x³=1, hence H̄=1; thus gcd(L̄,H̄)=1. Also H̄(0)=H̄(1)=1, so gcd(T̄,H̄)=1. These imply gcd(L,H)=gcd(T,H)=1 over Q: any nonconstant common divisor can be chosen monic integral because H has leading coefficient −1, and reduction preserves its positive degree, contradicting the displayed coprimalities. Hence 3N≡TL modulo H proves gcd(N,H)=1. Finally L is irreducible over Q because its discriminant is five; it divides neither 1+x nor H. The congruence 3N≡(1+x)H modulo L therefore proves gcd(N,L)=1. Consequently gcd(N,D)=1.

reasoning_steps.title: Minimality follows from the reduced rational function
reasoning_steps.argument: Any homogeneous constant-coefficient recurrence of order d over Q, valid for all sufficiently large indices, gives a polynomial Q(x)=1−c_1x−⋯−c_dx^d such that Q(x)A(x) is a polynomial: sufficiently high coefficients vanish by the recurrence. With A=N/D reduced, this implies D divides Q in Q[x], because D divides QN and gcd(N,D)=1. Therefore d≥deg D=8. The proved order-eight recurrence attains that bound. This is an additional theorem beyond the original requirements and beyond what the preceding extract claimed to establish.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the weighted enumerator and justify gap removal
reasoning_steps.argument: For n≥0, let P_n(q)=∑_S q^{∑_{i∈S}i}, where S ranges over subsets of {1,…,n} having no consecutive elements. The empty subset contributes 1. Define G_{N,k}(q)=∑_{0≤j_1<⋯<j_k<N}q^{∑j_h−k(k−1)/2}, the Gaussian binomial polynomial, with G_{N,0}=1. For a nonconsecutive k-subset i_1<⋯<i_k, the transformation y_h=i_h−(h−1) is a bijection onto ordinary k-subsets of {1,…,n−k+1}: its inverse i_h=y_h+h−1 has gaps at least two. Writing j_h=y_h−1 gives ∑i_h=∑j_h+k(k+1)/2. Combining this shift with the Gaussian normalization gives P_n(q)=∑_{k=0}^{⌊(n+1)/2⌋}q^{k²}G_{n−k+1,k}(q). This includes n=0 and k=0.

reasoning_steps.title: Obtain an exact recurrence and the total number of admissible subsets
reasoning_steps.argument: Partition the subsets according to whether n is selected. Excluding n leaves an arbitrary admissible subset on n−1 positions. Including n forces n−1 to be absent; removing n leaves an arbitrary admissible subset on n−2 positions and removes weight q^n. These disjoint reversible constructions prove P_n(q)=P_{n−1}(q)+q^nP_{n−2}(q) for n≥2, with P_0(q)=1 and P_1(q)=1+q. At q=1 this is the Fibonacci recurrence with initial values 1,2, so P_n(1)=F_{n+2}. For low-index checks, P_2(q)=1+q+q² and P_3(q)=1+q+q²+q³+q⁴, agreeing with direct enumeration.

reasoning_steps.title: Evaluate the cube-root contribution in every phase
reasoning_steps.argument: Let ω be a primitive cube root of unity, so 1+ω+ω²=0, and put p_n=P_n(ω). We prove, for all m≥0, p_{3m}=F_{m+1}+ωF_m, p_{3m+1}=(1+ω)F_{m+1}, and p_{3m+2}=F_m. The base triple is p_0=1, p_1=1+ω, p_2=0, matching F_0=0 and F_1=F_2=1. Suppose the formulas hold for m. The weighted recurrence gives p_{3m+3}=p_{3m+2}+p_{3m+1}=F_{m+2}+ωF_{m+1}. Next, p_{3m+4}=p_{3m+3}+ωp_{3m+2}=F_{m+2}+ω(F_{m+1}+F_m)=(1+ω)F_{m+2}. Finally, p_{3m+5}=p_{3m+4}+ω²p_{3m+3}=(1+ω+ω²)F_{m+2}+ω³F_{m+1}=F_{m+1}. Thus the complete next triple follows, proving all phases and all nonnegative indices.

reasoning_steps.title: Extract exactly the subsets whose sums are divisible by three
reasoning_steps.argument: For every integer h, (1+ω^h+ω^{2h})/3 is 1 when 3 divides h and 0 otherwise. Applying this identity termwise to the finite polynomial gives 3a_n=P_n(1)+P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²). Since P_n has integer coefficients, P_n(ω²) is the complex conjugate of P_n(ω). Define c_n=P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²). The formulas just proved and ω+ω²=−1 yield c_{3m}=2F_{m+1}−F_m, c_{3m+1}=F_{m+1}, and c_{3m+2}=2F_m. Consequently 3a_n=F_{n+2}+c_n exactly, including n=0 and the empty subset.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the constant-coefficient integer recurrence
reasoning_steps.argument: For each fixed residue r∈{0,1,2}, c_{3m+r} is a fixed linear combination of F_m and F_{m+1}. Hence c_{n+6}=c_{n+3}+c_n for every n≥0. Let E denote the forward shift, (Eu)_n=u_{n+1}. The sequences F_{n+2} and c_n are annihilated respectively by E²−E−1 and E⁶−E³−1. These shift polynomials commute, so their product annihilates their sum 3a_n and therefore a_n. Expanding gives (E²−E−1)(E⁶−E³−1)=E⁸−E⁷−E⁶−E⁵+E⁴+E³−E²+E+1. Thus, for every n≥0, a_{n+8}=a_{n+7}+a_{n+6}+a_{n+5}−a_{n+4}−a_{n+3}+a_{n+2}−a_{n+1}−a_n. Minimal order is not needed or claimed.

reasoning_steps.title: Give sufficient initial values and compute a_12
reasoning_steps.argument: For n=0,…,7, the values of F_{n+2} are (1,2,3,5,8,13,21,34), and the correction formulas give c_n=(2,1,0,1,1,2,3,2). Taking their sums and dividing by three gives (a_0,…,a_7)=(1,1,1,2,3,5,8,12). These eight consecutive values suffice because the recurrence is monic of order eight. At n=12=3·4, c_12=2F_5−F_4=10−3=7 and F_14=377, so a_12=(377+7)/3=128. As an arithmetic consistency check, the proved scalar recurrence gives a_8,…,a_12=(19,31,49,79,128).

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the limiting density with an exponential error bound
reasoning_steps.argument: Let φ=(1+√5)/2, so φ²=φ+1. For each r∈{0,1,2}, set b_m=c_{3m+r}. Its recurrence is b_{m+2}=b_{m+1}+b_m. The initial pairs are (2,1), (1,1), and (0,2), respectively, so |b_0|≤2 and |b_1|≤2φ. Induction using the triangle inequality gives |b_m|≤2φ^m: the induction step is 2φ^{m+1}+2φ^m=2φ^{m+2}. The last expression tends to zero, proving a_n/F_{n+2}→1/3 without assuming equidistribution.

These disjoint reversible constructions prove P_n(q)=P_{n−1}(q)+q^nP_{n−2}(q) for n≥2, with P_0(q)=1 and P_1(q)=1+q. At q=1 this is the Fibonacci recurrence with initial values 1,2, so P_n(1)=F_{n+2}. For low-index checks, P_2(q)=1+q+q² and P_3(q)=1+q+q²+q³+q⁴, agreeing with direct enumeration.

argument_steps.title: Evaluate the cube-root contribution in every phase
argument_steps.argument: Let ω be a primitive cube root of unity, so 1+ω+ω²=0, and put p_n=P_n(ω). We prove, for all m≥0, p_{3m}=F_{m+1}+ωF_m, p_{3m+1}=(1+ω)F_{m+1}, and p_{3m+2}=F_m. The base triple is p_0=1, p_1=1+ω, p_2=0, matching F_0=0 and F_1=F_2=1. Suppose the formulas hold for m. The weighted recurrence gives p_{3m+3}=p_{3m+2}+p_{3m+1}=F_{m+2}+ωF_{m+1}. Next, p_{3m+4}=p_{3m+3}+ωp_{3m+2}=F_{m+2}+ω(F_{m+1}+F_m)=(1+ω)F_{m+2}. Finally, p_{3m+5}=p_{3m+4}+ω²p_{3m+3}=(1+ω+ω²)F_{m+2}+ω³F_{m+1}=F_{m+1}. Thus the complete next triple follows, proving all phases and all nonnegative indices.

review.rationale: The base triple is (1,1+ω,0). For successive indices 3m+3, 3m+4, and 3m+5, the recurrence multipliers are respectively 1, ω, and ω². Substituting the proposed formulas gives exactly the next triple, using F_{m+2}=F_{m+1}+F_m and 1+ω+ω²=0. Thus induction covers every nonnegative index.

argument_steps.title: Extract exactly the subsets whose sums are divisible by three
argument_steps.argument: For every integer h, (1+ω^h+ω^{2h})/3 is 1 when 3 divides h and 0 otherwise. Applying this identity termwise to the finite polynomial gives 3a_n=P_n(1)+P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²). Since P_n has integer coefficients, P_n(ω²) is the complex conjugate of P_n(ω). Define c_n=P_n(ω)+P_n(ω²). The formulas just proved and ω+ω²=−1 yield c_{3m}=2F_{m+1}−F_m, c_{3m+1}=F_{m+1}, and c_{3m+2}=2F_m. Consequently 3a_n=F_{n+2}+c_n exactly, including n=0 and the empty subset.

solution_review.argument_summary: The include/exclude bijection gives weighted counting polynomials, and the cube-root filter expresses 3a_n as F_{n+2}+b_n. Formal functional equations give exact rational generating functions for b_n and a_n. Coefficient extraction proves the integer recurrence with its full index range, while initial correction values determine the eight initial counts and a_12. Exact Fibonacci formulas on the three residue subsequences bound the correction and prove the limit. Modular coprimality establishes reducedness and the additional minimal-order result.

argument_steps.title: Counting objects and the exact residue filter
argument_steps.argument: For n≥0, define P_n(q)=Σ_S q^{Σ_{i∈S}i}, where S ranges over subsets of {1,…,n} without consecutive elements. The empty subset contributes 1. For n≥2, excluding n contributes P_{n−1}(q); including it forbids n−1 and contributes q^nP_{n−2}(q). Thus P_n=P_{n−1}+q^nP_{n−2}, with P_0=1 and P_1=1+q. At q=1 these initial values and recurrence give P_n(1)=F_{n+2}. Fix a primitive cube root q. For every integer s, 1+q^s+q^{2s} is 3 if 3 divides s and 0 otherwise. Summing this identity over admissible subsets proves 3a_n=F_{n+2}+b_n, where b_n=P_n(q)+P_n(q²). This establishes the count directly rather than treating evaluation as coefficient extraction.

review.rationale: Including n leaves exactly an admissible subset on {1,…,n−2} and multiplies its weight by q^n. The initial polynomials include the empty subset. The cube-root sum selects precisely sums divisible by three, and the q=1 recurrence identifies F_{n+2}.

argument_steps.title: Check the latest finding's functional equations
argument_steps.argument: Work in Q(q)[[x]] and put G(x)=Σ_{n≥0}P_n(q)x^n. Summing the recurrence from n=2 gives G−1−(1+q)x=x(G−1)+q²x²G(qx). Therefore (1−x)G(x)=1+qx+q²x²G(qx). Substitution of qx and q²x gives (1−qx)G(qx)=1+q²x+qx²G(q²x) and (1−q²x)G(q²x)=1+x+x²G(x). These derivations account explicitly for n=0 and n=1 and require no negative-index convention.

review.rationale: Summation from n=2 leaves the initial contribution 1+qx after rearrangement. Substitution of qx and q²x, using q³=1, produces the other two equations with the displayed coefficients. No boundary term is missing.

argument_steps.title: Exact elimination, including the numerator
argument_steps.argument: Eliminate G(qx) and G(q²x) from those equations. The result is [(1−x)(1−qx)(1−q²x)−x⁶]G(x)=(1+qx)(1−qx)(1−q²x)+q²x²(1+q²x)(1−q²x)+x⁴(1+x). The three terms on the right expand respectively to 1−q²x−q²x²+qx³, q²x²−x⁴, and x⁴+x⁵. Since (1−x)(1−qx)(1−q²x)=1−x³, this proves G(x)=(1−q²x+qx³+x⁵)/(1−x³−x⁶). Each inverted series has constant term one, so the calculation is formal and does not assume analytic convergence.

review.rationale: Successive substitution gives a feedback term x⁶G(x). The three numerator contributions expand as stated and cancel in degrees two and four, leaving 1−q²x+qx³+x⁵. All divisions are legitimate in the formal-series ring because the denominators have constant term one.

argument_steps.title: Obtain the scalar generating function and recurrence
argument_steps.argument: Adding the identity for q to the one for q² gives B(x):=Σb_nx^n=(2+x−x³+2x⁵)/(1−x³−x⁶). The Fibonacci recurrence gives ΣF_{n+2}x^n=(1+x)/(1−x−x²). Hence the filter proves A(x):=Σa_nx^n=N(x)/D(x), where N=1−x²−x³+x⁵−x⁶−x⁷ and D=(1−x−x²)(1−x³−x⁶)=1−x−x²−x³+x⁴+x⁵−x⁶+x⁷+x⁸. In particular, [x^{n+8}]DA=0 for all n≥0 because deg N=7. This is exactly a_{n+8}−a_{n+7}−a_{n+6}−a_{n+5}+a_{n+4}+a_{n+3}−a_{n+2}+a_{n+1}+a_n=0. The index range follows from coefficient extraction, not extrapolation.

review.rationale: Adding the conjugate numerators gives 2+x−x³+2x⁵. Combining this fraction with the Fibonacci generating function gives exactly the stated N and D. Since deg N=7, coefficients of DA vanish from degree eight onward, proving the recurrence for every n≥0 with the stated signs.

argument_steps.title: Sufficient initial values and the exact requested count
argument_steps.argument: Comparing coefficients in (1−x³−x⁶)B=2+x−x³+2x⁵ gives (b_0,…,b_5)=(2,1,0,1,1,2) and b_{n+6}=b_{n+3}+b_n for n≥0. Thus b_6=3 and b_7=2. Together with (F_2,…,F_9)=(1,2,3,5,8,13,21,34), the filter yields (a_0,…,a_7)=(1,1,1,2,3,5,8,12). The recurrence is monic of order eight, so these determine all later values uniquely. Also b_9=b_6+b_3=4 and b_12=b_9+b_6=7. Since F_14=377, a_12=(377+7)/3=128.

review.rationale: Coefficient comparison gives b_0,…,b_5=(2,1,0,1,1,2) and the six-step recurrence. It yields b_6=3, b_7=2, b_9=4, and b_12=7. Applying the filter gives all eight initial counts and (377+7)/3=128. A monic order-eight recurrence is determined by those eight values.

argument_steps.title: Finite arithmetic check using integer residue counts
argument_steps.argument: Let C_n=(c_{n,0},c_{n,1},c_{n,2}) count admissible subsets by sum residue. The include/exclude bijection proves c_{n,r}=c_{n−1,r}+c_{n−2,(r−n) mod 3}, starting at C_0=(1,0,0) and C_1=(1,1,0). Successive substitution gives C_2=(1,1,1), C_3=(2,2,1), C_4=(3,3,2), C_5=(5,4,4), C_6=(8,7,6), C_7=(12,12,10), C_8=(19,18,18), C_9=(31,30,28), C_10=(49,49,46), C_11=(79,77,77), C_12=(128,126,123). For example, the last addition is C_12=C_11+C_10 because 12≡0 mod 3. This checks the initial counts, a_12 and the total 377. It is a finite arithmetic check sharing the original bijection, not independent empirical confirmation or a proof of the universal recurrence.

review.rationale: The residue shift r−n is required when n is included. The listed vectors satisfy that recurrence; in particular C_12=C_11+C_10=(128,126,123), with total 377. This is exact finite corroboration sharing the counting bijection, not independent evidence for the universal recurrence.

argument_steps.title: Exact correction on all three residue classes
argument_steps.argument: For each r∈{0,1,2}, k↦b_{3k+r} satisfies the Fibonacci recurrence. Its initial pairs are (2,1), (1,1), and (0,2), respectively. Each of the expressions 2F_{k+1}−F_k, F_{k+1}, and 2F_k satisfies that recurrence and matches its corresponding initial pair. Induction therefore proves b_{3k}=2F_{k+1}−F_k, b_{3k+1}=F_{k+1}, and b_{3k+2}=2F_k for every k≥0. Since 0≤F_k≤F_{k+1}, these formulas give 0≤b_n≤2F_{floor(n/3)+1}, including n=0 and the zero correction at n=2.

review.rationale: The six-step recurrence becomes the Fibonacci recurrence on each residue subsequence. Each proposed formula matches its two initial values, so induction proves all three formulas. Monotonicity and nonnegativity of Fibonacci numbers then give 0≤b_n≤2F_{floor(n/3)+1}, including n=0 and n=2.

argument_steps.title: New explicit error bound and the limit
argument_steps.argument: Let φ=(1+√5)/2, so φ²=φ+1. Induction from F_1=F_2=1 proves F_{k+1}≤φ^k for k≥0. A separate induction from F_2=1 and F_3=2≥φ proves F_{n+2}≥φ^n for n≥0; in both inductions the addition step uses φ²=φ+1. The filter and the preceding nonnegative bound consequently give 0≤a_n/F_{n+2}−1/3=b_n/(3F_{n+2})≤(2/3)φ^{floor(n/3)−n}≤(2/3)φ^{−2n/3}. The right side tends to zero, proving the limit. At n=0 the bound is attained, so the endpoint is explicitly covered.

review.rationale: Both Fibonacci inequalities follow from the stated two base cases and φ²=φ+1. Division is valid because F_{n+2}>0. Since floor(n/3)−n≤−2n/3 and φ>1, the resulting bound has the asserted direction and tends to zero. At n=0 both sides equal 2/3.

argument_steps.title: Test the cancellation objection without assuming modular degree preservation
argument_steps.argument: Write L=1−x−x², H=1−x³−x⁶ and T=2+x−x³+2x⁵. The already derived identity is 3N=(1+x)H+TL. Over F_2, L̄=1+x+x², H̄=1+x³+x⁶ and T̄=x(x+1)². Modulo L̄, x³=1, so H̄=1; hence gcd(L̄,H̄)=1. Also H̄(0)=H̄(1)=1, so gcd(T̄,H̄)=1. These imply gcd(L,H)=gcd(T,H)=1 over Q: any common rational factor can be normalized to a monic integer factor because −H is monic integral. Division of the other integer polynomial by that monic factor has integer quotient and remainder; rational divisibility forces the remainder to vanish. Reduction modulo two therefore produces a common monic factor of unchanged positive degree, a contradiction. This argument does not assume that T itself retains its degree modulo two. The identity for 3N now gives gcd(N,H)=1. Finally L is irreducible over Q, with discriminant five, and divides neither 1+x nor H. Reducing the same identity modulo L excludes L dividing N. Thus gcd(N,D)=1: the proposed cancellation counterexample is excluded.

review.rationale: Over F_2, H has remainder one modulo L and is nonzero at both roots of T=x(x+1)², proving both modular coprimalities. A rational common factor with H can be chosen monic integral; its integral divisibility into the other polynomial ensures reduction produces a common factor of unchanged positive degree. The identity for 3N then excludes common factors with H, while irreducibility of L excludes the remaining possible cancellation.

argument_steps.argument: Any homogeneous constant-coefficient recurrence over Q of order d, even if valid only eventually, gives a polynomial Q(x)=1−c_1x−⋯−c_dx^d for which Q(x)A(x) is polynomial: all sufficiently high coefficients vanish by the recurrence. As A=N/D is reduced, D divides QN and coprimality forces D to divide Q. Therefore d≥deg D=8, and the proved order-eight recurrence attains the bound. This retains the latest saved finding without treating its earlier model review as a premise. No mathematical correction to the supplied latest derivation was needed; the material addition here is the explicit uniform error estimate.

Consequently its order is at least eight, attained by the established recurrence. This proves the additional minimality claim without relying on prior reviewer agreement.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the weighted enumerator and justify gap removal
reasoning_steps.argument: For n≥0, let P_n(q)=∑_S q^{∑_{i∈S}i}, where S ranges over subsets of {1,…,n} having no consecutive elements. The empty subset contributes 1. For a nonconsecutive k-subset i_1<⋯<i_k, the transformation y_h=i_h−(h−1) is a bijection onto ordinary k-subsets of {1,…,n−k+1}: its inverse i_h=y_h+h−1 has gaps at least two. Writing j_h=y_h−1 gives ∑i_h=∑j_h+k(k+1)/2. Combining this shift with the Gaussian normalization gives P_n(q)=∑_{k=0}^{⌊(n+1)/2⌋}q^{k²}G_{n−k+1,k}(q). This includes n=0 and k=0.

review.rationale: The transformation y_h=i_h−(h−1) preserves the endpoint constraints and converts gaps of at least two into strict increases, with the stated inverse. At q=1 this is the Fibonacci recurrence with initial values 1,2, so P_n(1)=F_{n+2}. For low-index checks, P_2(q)=1+q+q² and P_3(q)=1+q+q²+q³+q⁴, agreeing with direct enumeration.
